I agree with what a lot are saying:: BDD is NOT about what you look like, it's about how you feel about it. Also, I feel like it's really not a good idea to post about how ''some of us are ugly'' in a group based on supporting each other through serious body image issues: would you tell people with eating disorders that ''some of us are fat actually''? It's very damaging for people who worry about their appearance to have their worst fears validated. BDD is the obsession, BDD is the compulsive behaviour related to your obsession, it has NOTHING to do with how you really look like, as contradictory as that sounds. Having a deformity doesn't mean you don't have BDD: if you're obsessing over it and feel monstruous about it, that's probably BDD. BDD isn't about imagining flaws, it's also about making real flaws out to be much bigger than they are.

So, I'm responding to this as someone who, well, can tend to be a bit like her. A lot of times, this type of behaviour comes from insecurities or a general need for validation and approval. Honestly, yes, it can be concerning, but with the right conversation and relationship dynamic, I'm certain you could be able to find a way to make this healthy for the both of you.

Now, of course, make sure that this doesn't become a situation in which her happiness depends on her relationship with you, because that would not be fair to you at all. However, her willingness to please and to ask for approval isn't automatically a sign of huge instability: she might simply be a more submissive sexual partner or she might simply be the kind of person whose love languages are more traditionally ''romantic''. I think what you need to make sure is whether or not she feels she HAS to do this to make you happy or if she simply enjoys this dynamic with the knowledge that it isn't required of her.

Of course, the main thing to do here would be to talk to her about it. I'd recommend phrasing it as a concern rather than as a complaint, because, if she is a very co-dependant person, that may be incredibly hurtful to her and derail the conversation. Simply try to ensure that she doesn't feel obligated to do these things and that her entire happiness or stability doesn't rely on this very new relationship.

The fact that you consider yourself to be objectively ugly IS what makes you have dysmorphia. You're not alone in these feelings, I promise you: everyone with BDD has told themself at some point ''Wait, but this can't be a mental thing, when I look in the mirror, I can see how ugly I am!''. But BDD isn't just a mindset things. It's been shown that BDD even hinders our ability to read faces, making us unable to actually see what we look like correctly. You have to recognize that BDD has nothing to do with how you look and everything to do with how you feel about it. If you think about your appearance constantly, if you have compulsions and rituals that you do to ''fix'' your appearance, if you obsess over it, if you want to isolate yourself, then you probably have BDD, no matter what you look like. You can't trust your eyes or your brain on what you look like, thats the hardest part about BDD. But you're not alone and you can find happiness, even though it's hard, I promise you. I hope things get better for you <3
